banana-slug: Deep damp leaves, mossy shade and mushrooms to graze. Skip the pond — this one drinks through its skin, straight out of the litter.
forest-salamander: This one skips the tadpole stage completely — the eggs hatch fully formed inside a rotting log. No pond needed, just damp wood and deep leaves.
black-bear: A full larder and a winter bed: heavy berry crops, acorn-bearing oaks, water, and a den under the tipped-up roots of a fallen tree.
great-horned-owl: Tall trees holding somebody else's old nest — this one never builds its own — and prey already back in the woods.
prairie-vole: Thick unmown grass with clipped runways beneath it. This one arrives early, and almost everything with teeth or talons is waiting on it.
western-meadowlark: Wide unbroken native grass and a perch to sing from. Skip the shrubs here — woody cover is exactly what pushes this one out.
red-tailed-hawk: A tall tree crown for the stick nest, open grass to hunt over, and a meadow already full of small mammals. It takes its water from its prey.
sandhill-crane: This one wants space and quiet. Build a wide, well-balanced marsh and heap a nest mound up above the waterline.
great-blue-heron: Shallow water full of fish and frogs, and a stand of tall trees for the colony. This one nests alongside its own kind or not at all.
bighorn-sheep: Good grazing is only half of it. It will not use a slope it cannot escape from, so put the turf right up against broken cliff — and a mineral lick nearby, because it will travel a long way for salt.
snowshoe-hare: Low tangled cover it can freeze motionless inside, a scraped hollow under the krummholz to sit out the day, and willow to browse in winter. Open ground with a rock pile on it is the opposite of what it wants. It eats snow instead of drinking.
white-tailed-ptarmigan: Willow is the whole winter for this one, and a soft deep drift is its bedroom. It eats snow instead of drinking, and it has no use at all for a flower planter.
gray-crowned-rosy-finch: Rock with cracks in it, not a heap of stones. This one nests inside the cliff, feeds out across the scree, and drinks meltwater.
mountain-chickadee: Dead trees are the point. An old woodpecker hole is both shelter and a starting place — this one takes a ready-made cavity and works it wider. The whitebark pines come from its forgotten seeds.
pine-marten: You cannot build this one's habitat out of rocks and flowers. It needs a stand of real trees, dead wood on the ground, and hares already living there.
golden-eagle: This one comes last, when the mountain is properly alive again. It needs a real cliff for the eyrie and open ground below with plenty moving on it.
purple-sea-urchin: Kelp first — it has to have something to eat. Then think hard about what is going to eat it.
gray-whale: Give this one deep water and a seabed thick with tiny shrimp-like amphipods. Tidepools and dune plantings will never bring it in.
sea-otter: Living kelp forest to wrap up in, calm water to groom in, and urchins and shellfish to eat. Dead kelp on the sand is no use to it.
harbor-seal: Deep water to fish in and quiet rocks to haul out on, with room around them. A haul-out is not a bird nesting closure — build the right thing.
antelope-squirrel: Dry seeds alone will not keep it alive — it needs juicy fruit, and that means welcoming the bees first.
cactus-wren: Cholla is the nest. Nothing else out here is spiny enough, and it never once needs a drink.
burrowing-owl: It cannot dig. Bring the tortoise back first and its old den becomes the front door — with low, open ground out front to hunt over.
praying-mantis: Leave stiff dead stems standing through the winter. That's where the foam egg case is glued, and cutting them back in autumn cuts next summer's brood.
marsh-wren: Bulrush and cattail standing in water — stiff stems it can weave a hanging ball nest between.
barn-owl: A dark loft or a deep box up off the ground, wide grass to quarter over, and a meadow already full of voles. It takes its water from its prey.
mountain-goat: Steeper is better. Give it cliff ledges to bed on, turf to graze between them, and a mineral lick, because it will travel for hours to eat salty ground. Do not expect one out on the open flats.
bottlenose-dolphin: Deep water to travel through, cold currents and kelp edges to hold the fish, and a real breaking surf line, because that is where this one does its hunting.
desert-tarantula: Firm ground it can line with silk, and then quiet. A burrow it digs is one she may still be sitting in twenty years from now.
desert-hawk: One bird is never the whole story. A family needs a tall cactus strong enough to hold the nest, high lookouts all around it, and open ground with rabbits crossing it.
water-strider: This one needs calm. Find a pocket of water the wind cannot ruffle, with floating stems on it to rest and lay eggs on.
blue-jay: Oaks and a patch of soft open ground to bury the acorns in. Some of the ones it forgets will be your next oak trees.
wood-frog: A pool that dries up in summer is the good kind — no fish means the tadpoles live. Keep deep leaves nearby for them to freeze in.
river-cooter: Logs in the sun to bask on and a bare warm bank to bury eggs in. One that cannot get warm cannot digest its dinner.
black-swift: Find the wettest, darkest crack in the cliff and keep the water running down it. This one will not nest anywhere it can walk to.
